nodes.name: Frame
nodes.statement: A \emph{frame} is a complete lattice $(L, \leq)$ satisfying the infinite distributive law (frame distributivity): $$a \land \bigvee_{i \in I} b_i = \bigvee_{i \in I} (a \land b_i)$$ for all $a \in L$ and all families $(b_i)_{i \in I}$ of elements of $L$.
differentia: satisfying the infinite distributive law (frame distributivity)
nodes.label: def:frame

nodes.name: Frame Homomorphism
nodes.statement: A map $f: L \to M$ between frames is a \emph{frame homomorphism} if it: \begin{enumerate} \item Preserves arbitrary joins: $f(\bigvee_{i \in I} a_i) = \bigvee_{i \in I} f(a_i)$ \item Preserves finite meets: $f(a \land b) = f(a) \land f(b)$ and $f(\top) = \top$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:frame-homomorphism

nodes.name: Frame homomorphisms need not preserve bottom; category Frame
nodes.statement: Note that frame homomorphisms need not preserve $\bot$. The category of frames and frame homomorphisms is denoted $\mathbf{Frame}$.
nodes.statement_short: Frame homomorphisms need not preserve $\bot$; frames and their homomorphisms form the category $\mathbf{Frame}$.
nodes.label: remark:frame-homomorphism-bottom

nodes.name: Locale
nodes.statement: A \emph{locale} is a formal dual of a frame. The category $\mathbf{Loc}$ has: \begin{enumerate} \item Objects: Frames (understood as the lattice of open sets of a generalized space) \item Morphisms: $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(X, Y) := \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Frame}}(\mathcal{O}(Y), \mathcal{O}(X))$ (contravariant) \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A locale is a frame viewed contravariantly; Loc-morphisms X→Y are frame homomorphisms O(Y)→O(X).
nodes.label: def:locale

nodes.name: Locale Morphism Composition
nodes.statement: Composition of locale morphisms is well-defined and associative.
conclusions: Composition of locale morphisms is well-defined and associative.
nodes.label: lemma:locale-morphism-composition

nodes.name: Presented Frame
nodes.statement: A frame presented by a set of generators $G$ and a set of relations $R$ is denoted: $$\mathrm{Fr}\langle G \mid R \rangle$$ This is the free frame on generators $G$ quotiented by the frame congruence generated by $R$.
nodes.statement_short: Fr⟨G|R⟩ is the free frame on generators G quotiented by the congruence generated by relations R.
nodes.label: def:presented-frame

nodes.name: Universal Property of Presented Frames
nodes.statement: Let $L = \mathrm{Fr}\langle G \mid R \rangle$ be a presented frame, and let $M$ be another frame. A frame homomorphism $f: L \to M$ is determined by: \begin{enumerate} \item A function $\phi: G \to M$ \item A verification that the relations $R$ are respected: for every relation in $R$, $\phi$ satisfies it in $M$ \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $L = \mathrm{Fr}\langle G \mid R \rangle$ be a presented frame, and let $M$ be another frame.
nodes.statement_short: A frame homomorphism out of Fr⟨G|R⟩ is determined by a map on generators respecting the relations.
nodes.label: lemma:universal-property-presented-frame

nodes.name: Characterization by Generators and Relations
nodes.statement: A frame homomorphism from a presented frame is completely determined by its action on generators.
conclusions: A frame homomorphism from a presented frame is completely determined by its action on generators.
nodes.label: cor:characterization-presented-frame

nodes.name: Formalization Approach
nodes.statement: \textbf{Implementation note:} Instead of formalizing the full abstract theory of frame presentations (which would require constructing free frames and frame congruences), we use a concrete approach for the Zariski locale. For the frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ of radical ideals, we prove: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Generation:} Every radical ideal is the supremum of basic opens: $$I = \bigvee_{f \in I} D(f)$$ This is \texttt{Rad.radical\_eq\_sSup\_basicOpen}. \item \textbf{Universal property:} A frame homomorphism from $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is uniquely determined by its action on basic opens: $$(\forall f \in R,\, \varphi(D(f)) = \psi(D(f))) \implies \varphi = \psi$$ This is \texttt{Rad.frameHom\_eq\_of\_basicOpen\_eq}. \end{enumerate} These concrete theorems provide the same practical power as the abstract presentation $\mathrm{Fr}\langle D(f) : f \in R \mid \text{relations} \rangle$ without requiring the full infrastructure of quotients of free frames.
nodes.statement_short: The formalization avoids abstract frame presentations, proving instead that radical ideals are joins of basic opens and frame homs are determined on basic opens.
nodes.label: remark:concrete-approach

nodes.name: Radical Ideal
nodes.statement: An ideal $I \triangleleft R$ of a commutative ring $R$ is \emph{radical} if $I = \sqrt{I}$, where $$\sqrt{I} := \{x \in R : \exists n \geq 1, x^n \in I\}$$ The set of all radical ideals of $R$ is denoted $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.genus: ideal $I \triangleleft R$ of a commutative ring $R$
nodes.label: def:radical-ideal

nodes.name: Order and Operations on Radical Ideals
nodes.statement: For radical ideals $I, J \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Order:} $I \leq J :\iff I \subseteq J$ (set inclusion) \item \textbf{Meet (Infimum):} $I \land J := I \cap J$ (intersection) \item \textbf{Join (Supremum):} For a family $(I_i)_{i \in I}$, we define $\bigvee_i I_i := \sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$ \item \textbf{Top:} $\top := R$ (the whole ring, which is radical) \item \textbf{Bottom:} $\bot := \sqrt{(0)} = \mathrm{Nil}(R)$ (the nilradical) \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Rad(R) is ordered by inclusion, with meet = intersection, join = radical of the sum, top = R, bottom = nilradical.
nodes.label: def:radical-ideal-operations

nodes.name: Intersection of Radical Ideals is Radical
nodes.statement: If $I, J \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$, then $I \cap J \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
conclusions: $I \cap J \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$
nodes.label: lemma:intersection-radical

nodes.name: Arbitrary Intersections are Radical
nodes.statement: If $(I_i)_{i \in I}$ is a family of radical ideals, then $\bigcap_{i \in I} I_i$ is radical.
assumptions: $(I_i)_{i \in I}$ is a family of radical ideals
conclusions: $\bigcap_{i \in I} I_i$ is radical
nodes.label: cor:arbitrary-intersection-radical

nodes.name: Join of Radical Ideals
nodes.statement: For a family $(I_i)_{i \in I}$ of radical ideals, $\sqrt{\sum_{i \in I} I_i}$ is the supremum in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
assumptions: For a family $(I_i)_{i \in I}$ of radical ideals
conclusions: $\sqrt{\sum_{i \in I} I_i}$ is the supremum in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$
nodes.label: lemma:join-radical-ideals

nodes.name: Radical Ideals Form a Complete Lattice
nodes.statement: The structure $(\mathrm{Rad}(R), \leq, \land, \bigvee, \top, \bot)$ with operations as in \Cref{def:radical-ideal-operations} forms a complete lattice.
conclusions: forms a complete lattice
nodes.label: thm:radical-complete-lattice

nodes.name: Product of Ideals and Radical
nodes.statement: For ideals $I, J \triangleleft R$: $$\sqrt{I \cdot J} = \sqrt{I \cap J}$$
conclusions: $$\sqrt{I \cdot J} = \sqrt{I \cap J}$$
nodes.label: lemma:product-radical-property

nodes.name: Frame Distributivity of Radical Ideals
nodes.statement: The complete lattice $(\mathrm{Rad}(R), \leq, \land, \bigvee, \top, \bot)$ satisfies the infinite distributive law: $$I \land \bigvee_{j \in J} K_j = \bigvee_{j \in J} (I \land K_j)$$ for all $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ and all families $(K_j)_{j \in J}$ of radical ideals.
assumptions: for all $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ and all families $(K_j)_{j \in J}$ of radical ideals
nodes.statement_short: Rad(R) satisfies the infinite distributive law $I \land \bigvee_j K_j = \bigvee_j (I \land K_j)$.
nodes.label: thm:radical-frame-distributivity

nodes.name: Radical Ideals Form a Frame
nodes.statement: The structure $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is a frame.
conclusions: The structure $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is a frame.
nodes.label: cor:radical-frame

nodes.name: Basic Open Sets
nodes.statement: For $f \in R$, define the \emph{basic open set} (in the Zariski locale): $$D(f) := \sqrt{(f)} \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$$ where $(f)$ is the principal ideal generated by $f$.
nodes.statement_short: $D(f)$ is the radical of the principal ideal $(f)$, the basic open of the Zariski locale.
nodes.label: def:basic-open-set

nodes.name: Basic Opens are Radical
nodes.statement: For any $f \in R$, the ideal $D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$ is radical.
conclusions: the ideal $D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$ is radical
nodes.label: lemma:basic-open-radical

nodes.name: Properties of Basic Opens
nodes.statement: The basic opens satisfy: \begin{enumerate} \item $D(1) = \sqrt{(1)} = R = \top$ \item $D(0) = \sqrt{(0)} = \sqrt{\{0\}} = \{x : \exists n, x^n = 0\} = \bot$ (the nilradical) \item $D(fg) = D(f) \land D(g)$ \item $D(f^n) = D(f)$ for all $n \geq 1$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lemma:basic-open-properties

nodes.name: Meet and Join of Basic Opens
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item $D(f) \land D(g) = D(fg)$ \item $D(f) \lor D(g) = \sqrt{D(f) + D(g)} = D(f) \lor D(g)$ (not generally a basic open) \item More generally, for a family $(f_i)_{i \in I}$: $\bigvee_i D(f_i) = \sqrt{(f_i : i \in I)}$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Meets of basic opens are basic opens $D(fg)$; joins are radicals of generated ideals.
nodes.label: lemma:basic-open-meet-join

nodes.name: Radical Membership and Basic Opens
nodes.statement: For $f \in R$ and $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$: $$f \in \sqrt{I} \iff D(f) \subseteq I \iff D(f) \leq I$$
nodes.label: lemma:radical-membership-basic-open

nodes.name: Cover Criterion for Basic Opens
nodes.statement: For $f \in R$ and a family $(g_i)_{i \in I}$ of elements of $R$: $$D(f) \leq \bigvee_i D(g_i) \iff f \in \sqrt{(g_i : i \in I)}$$
assumptions: For $f \in R$ and a family $(g_i)_{i \in I}$ of elements of $R$:
nodes.statement_short: $D(f)$ is covered by the $D(g_i)$ iff $f$ lies in the radical of the ideal they generate.
nodes.label: lemma:cover-criterion-basic-opens

nodes.name: Frame Presentation of Spec(R)
nodes.statement: The Zariski frame of a commutative ring $R$ admits the presentation: $$\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{Spec}\, R) \cong \mathrm{Fr}\langle D(f) : f \in R \mid \mathcal{R} \rangle$$ where the relations $\mathcal{R}$ are: \begin{enumerate} \item $D(1) = \top$ \item $D(0) = \bot$ \item $D(fg) = D(f) \land D(g)$ \item $D(f^n) = D(f)$ for all $n \geq 1$ \item For any family $(f_i)_{i \in I}$ with $1 \in (f_i : i \in I)$: $\bigvee_i D(f_i) = \top$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.4 Frame Presentation of the Zariski Locale
nodes.statement_short: The Zariski frame of $R$ is presented by generators $D(f)$ subject to unit, zero, multiplicativity, power and covering relations.
nodes.label: thm:zariski-frame-presentation

nodes.name: Pushforward of Ideals
nodes.statement: For a ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$ and an ideal $I \triangleleft R$, the pushforward is: $$\phi(I) := \phi(I) \cdot S = \{\sum_j \phi(a_j) s_j : a_j \in I, s_j \in S\}$$ This is the ideal of $S$ generated by $\phi(I)$.
nodes.label: def:pushforward-ideals

nodes.name: Induced Frame Homomorphism
nodes.statement: For a ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$, define: $$\phi^*: \mathrm{Rad}(R) \to \mathrm{Rad}(S)$$ by: $$\phi^*(I) := \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S}$$ for each radical ideal $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\phi:R\to S$, $\phi^*(I)$ is the radical of the extension of $I$ to $S$.
nodes.label: def:induced-frame-homomorphism

nodes.name: Image of Radical is Radical
nodes.statement: If $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$, then $\phi^*(I) = \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \in \mathrm{Rad}(S)$.
conclusions: $\phi^*(I) = \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \in \mathrm{Rad}(S)$
nodes.label: lemma:radical-image

nodes.name: Preservation of Finite Meets
nodes.statement: For $I, J \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$: $$\phi^*(I \land J) = \phi^*(I) \land \phi^*(J)$$
nodes.label: lemma:preserve-finite-meets

nodes.name: Preservation of Arbitrary Joins
nodes.statement: For a family $(I_j)_{j \in J}$ of radical ideals: $$\phi^*(\bigvee_j I_j) = \bigvee_j \phi^*(I_j)$$
assumptions: For a family $(I_j)_{j \in J}$ of radical ideals:
nodes.label: lemma:preserve-arbitrary-joins

nodes.name: $\phi^*$ is a Frame Homomorphism
nodes.statement: For a ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$, the map $\phi^*: \mathrm{Rad}(R) \to \mathrm{Rad}(S)$ is a frame homomorphism.
assumptions: For a ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$
conclusions: the map $\phi^*: \mathrm{Rad}(R) \to \mathrm{Rad}(S)$ is a frame homomorphism
nodes.label: thm:phi-star-frame-homomorphism

nodes.name: Identity Homomorphism
nodes.statement: For the identity ring homomorphism $\mathrm{id}_R : R \to R$: $$(\mathrm{id}_R)^* = \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Rad}(R)}$$
assumptions: For the identity ring homomorphism $\mathrm{id}_R : R \to R$:
nodes.label: lemma:identity-homomorphism

nodes.name: Functoriality of Spec
nodes.statement: There exists a contravariant functor: $$\mathrm{Spec}: \mathbf{CRing}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Loc}$$ defined by: \begin{enumerate} \item Objects: $\mathrm{Spec}(R) := \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ (viewed as a locale) \item Morphisms: For $\phi: R \to S$ in $\mathbf{CRing}$, $\mathrm{Spec}(\phi) := (\phi^*)^{\mathrm{op}}: \mathrm{Spec}(S) \to \mathrm{Spec}(R)$ \end{enumerate} with: \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathrm{id}_R) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}(R)}$ \item For $\phi: R \to S$ and $\psi: S \to T$: $\mathrm{Spec}(\psi \circ \phi) = \mathrm{Spec}(\phi) \circ \mathrm{Spec}(\psi)$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Spec is a contravariant functor from commutative rings to locales, sending $R$ to Rad(R) and $\phi$ to $(\phi^*)^{op}$.
nodes.label: thm:functoriality-spec

nodes.name: Sheaf on a Locale
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a frame (viewed as a category with objects being elements of $L$ and morphisms being the order relations $u \leq v$). A \emph{sheaf on $L$ with values in a category $\mathcal{C}$} is a functor $\mathcal{F}: L^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathcal{C}$ such that for every family $(u_i)_{i \in I}$ with $\bigvee_i u_i = u$: $$\mathcal{F}(u) \to \prod_i \mathcal{F}(u_i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} \mathcal{F}(u_i \land u_j)$$ is an equalizer diagram in $\mathcal{C}$.
nodes.definiendum: sheaf on $L$ with values in a category $\mathcal{C}$
nodes.statement_short: A $\mathcal C$-valued sheaf on a frame is a presheaf satisfying the equalizer condition for every cover.
nodes.label: def:sheaf-locale

nodes.name: Sheaf Exactness
nodes.statement: The equalizer condition states that a section $s \in \mathcal{F}(u)$ is uniquely determined by its restrictions to the basic opens $(u_i)_{i \in I}$, and any compatible family of sections on the opens glues to a unique global section.
nodes.statement_short: The equalizer condition means sections are determined by restrictions and compatible families glue uniquely.
nodes.label: remark:sheaf-exactness

nodes.name: Localization of a Ring at an Element
nodes.statement: For $f \in R$, define $R_f$ as the localization of $R$ at the multiplicative set $\{1, f, f^2, \ldots\}$: $$R_f := \{r/f^k : r \in R, k \in \mathbb{N}\}$$ with the obvious ring operations.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
differentia: at the multiplicative set $\{1, f, f^2, \ldots\}$
nodes.label: def:localization-element

nodes.name: Basic Properties of Localizations
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item There is a canonical ring homomorphism $\iota_f: R \to R_f$ sending $r \mapsto r/1$. \item If $f$ is a unit in $R$, then $R_f = R$. \item If $f$ is nilpotent, then $R_f$ is the zero ring. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: $R\to R_f$ is a ring map; $R_f=R$ if $f$ is a unit; $R_f=0$ if $f$ is nilpotent.

conclusions: There is a canonical ring homomorphism $\iota_f: R \to R_f$ sending $r \mapsto r/1$.
$R_f = R$
$R_f$ is the zero ring

nodes.label: lemma:localization-properties

nodes.name: Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locale
nodes.statement: Define $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R}$ on the basic opens by: $$\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R}(D(f)) := R_f$$ For a inclusion $D(f) \leq D(g)$ (i.e., $f \in \sqrt{(g)}$, so $f^n = rg$ for some $r$ and $n \geq 1$): $$\rho_{g,f}: R_g \to R_f, \quad \frac{a}{g^k} \mapsto \frac{a r^k}{f^{nk}}$$
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: The structure sheaf assigns $R_f$ to $D(f)$, with restriction maps $\rho_{g,f}:R_g\to R_f$ when $D(f)\le D(g)$.
nodes.label: def:structure-sheaf-zariski

nodes.name: Restriction Maps are Well-Defined
nodes.statement: For $f \in \sqrt{(g)}$ (so $f^n = rg$), the map $\rho_{g,f}$ is a well-defined ring homomorphism. (Well-definedness is automatic from using \texttt{IsLocalization.Away.lift}.)
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
conclusions: the map $\rho_{g,f}$ is a well-defined ring homomorphism
nodes.label: lemma:restriction-maps-well-defined

nodes.name: Restriction Maps Compose
nodes.statement: For $D(f) \leq D(g) \leq D(h)$, the restriction maps satisfy: $$\rho_{h,f} = \rho_{g,f} \circ \rho_{h,g}$$
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.label: lemma:restriction-compose

nodes.name: Extension to Arbitrary Radical Ideals
nodes.statement: For a radical ideal $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$, extend the structure sheaf by: $$\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R}(I) := \lim_{f \in I} R_f$$ the inverse limit of localizations as $f$ ranges over $I$. For $I \leq J$ (i.e., $I \subseteq J$), the restriction map is induced by the universal property of limits.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: On a radical ideal $I$, the structure sheaf is the inverse limit of $R_f$ over $f\in I$.
nodes.label: def:structure-sheaf-radical-ideals

nodes.name: Sheaf Property of the Structure Sheaf
nodes.statement: The structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R}$ is a sheaf on the Zariski locale $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
conclusions: The structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R}$ is a sheaf on the Zariski locale $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.label: thm:structure-sheaf-property

nodes.name: Completely Prime Filter
nodes.statement: A \emph{completely prime filter} on a frame $L$ is a filter $F \subseteq L$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $\top \in F$ (contains the top element) \item $F$ is upward closed: if $u \in F$ and $u \leq v$, then $v \in F$ \item $F$ is closed under meets: if $u, v \in F$, then $u \land v \in F$ \item $F$ is completely prime: for any family $(u_i)_{i \in I}$, if $\bigvee_i u_i \in F$ then $\exists i, u_i \in F$ \end{enumerate} Completely prime filters correspond to ``points'' of the locale in pointless topology.
nodes.label: def:completely-prime-filter

nodes.name: Prime Ideals Correspond to Filters
nodes.statement: For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of a commutative ring $R$, the set $$F_{\mathfrak{p}} := \{I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R) : \exists f \in I, f \notin \mathfrak{p}\}$$ forms a completely prime filter on $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$. This establishes the correspondence: points of $\mathrm{Spec}\, R$ $\leftrightarrow$ prime ideals of $R$.
assumptions: For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of a commutative ring $R$
conclusions: forms a completely prime filter on $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$
nodes.statement_short: Each prime $\mathfrak p$ gives a completely prime filter $F_{\mathfrak p}$ on Rad(R): points of Spec R are primes.
nodes.label: thm:prime-ideal-to-filter

nodes.name: Locally Ringed Locale
nodes.statement: A \emph{locally ringed locale} is a triple $(X, \mathcal{O}_X, \text{stalks\_local})$ where: \begin{enumerate} \item $X$ is a locale (a frame) \item $\mathcal{O}_X$ is a presheaf of rings on $X$ \item For every completely prime filter $F$ on $X$, the stalk $\mathcal{O}_{X,F}$ is a local ring \end{enumerate}
differentia: $\mathcal{O}_X$ is a presheaf of rings on $X$
For every completely prime filter $F$ on $X$, the stalk $\mathcal{O}_{X,F}$ is a local ring
nodes.label: def:locally-ringed-locale

nodes.name: Stalk in a Locale
nodes.statement: For a sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on a locale $X$ and an element $u \in X$, the \emph{stalk} is defined as: $$\mathcal{F}_{\bar{u}} := \lim_{v \in \downarrow u} \mathcal{F}(v)$$ where $\downarrow u := \{v \in X : v \leq u\}$ is the principal order filter at $u$.
nodes.statement_short: The stalk of $\mathcal F$ at $u$ is the limit of $\mathcal F(v)$ over $v\le u$.
nodes.label: def:stalk-locale

nodes.name: Stalks at Prime Elements
nodes.statement: When $u$ is a prime element in the frame (which exists for frames arising as radical ideals), the stalk has better properties. In the Zariski locale, these correspond to prime ideals.
nodes.label: remark:stalks-prime-elements

nodes.name: Stalk at a Prime Ideal
nodes.statement: For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $R$, the stalk of the structure sheaf at $\mathfrak{p}$ is the localization: $$\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec}\, R, \mathfrak{p}} := R_{\mathfrak{p}} = \mathrm{Localization.AtPrime}\, \mathfrak{p}$$ This is a local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p} R_{\mathfrak{p}}$.
nodes.label: def:stalk-at-prime

nodes.name: Stalk at Prime is Local
nodes.statement: For any prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$, the stalk $R_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a local ring. This is provided by \texttt{Localization.AtPrime.isLocalRing} from Mathlib.
conclusions: the stalk $R_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a local ring
nodes.label: thm:stalk-at-prime-local

nodes.name: Affine Scheme
nodes.statement: An \emph{affine scheme} is a locally ringed locale of the form $(\mathrm{Spec} R, \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R})$ for some commutative ring $R$, where: \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{Spec} R = \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is the Zariski locale \item $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R}$ is the structure sheaf constructed in \Cref{def:structure-sheaf-zariski} \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:affine-scheme

nodes.name: Structure Presheaf of Affine Scheme
nodes.statement: For an affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec}\, R$, the structure presheaf is defined as: $$\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec}\, R}(I) := \mathrm{Spec.sheafExtend}\, I$$ for each radical ideal $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.label: def:structure-presheaf-affine

nodes.name: Affine Schemes are Locally Ringed
nodes.statement: Every affine scheme $(\mathrm{Spec} R, \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R})$ is a locally ringed locale.
conclusions: Every affine scheme $(\mathrm{Spec} R, \mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R})$ is a locally ringed locale.
nodes.label: thm:affine-scheme-locally-ringed

nodes.name: Morphism of Affine Schemes
nodes.statement: A morphism of affine schemes from $\mathrm{Spec} R$ to $\mathrm{Spec} S$ is a morphism of locally ringed locales, i.e., a pair $(f_{\#}, f^{\sharp})$ where: \begin{enumerate} \item $f_{\#}: \mathrm{Spec} R \to \mathrm{Spec} S$ is a locale morphism (i.e., a frame homomorphism $f_{\#}^*: \mathrm{Rad}(S) \to \mathrm{Rad}(R)$) \item $f^{\sharp}: \mathcal{O}_S \to f_{\#*} \mathcal{O}_R$ is a morphism of sheaves of rings respecting the local ring structure \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A morphism Spec R → Spec S is a locale morphism with a compatible map of structure sheaves.
nodes.label: def:morphism-affine-schemes

nodes.name: Ring Homomorphisms Induce Scheme Morphisms
nodes.statement: Every ring homomorphism $\phi: S \to R$ induces a morphism of affine schemes: $$\mathrm{Spec} \phi: \mathrm{Spec} R \to \mathrm{Spec} S$$
nodes.label: thm:ring-hom-to-scheme-morphism

nodes.name: Scheme (Pointfree)
nodes.statement: A \emph{scheme} is a locally ringed locale $(X, \mathcal{O}_X)$ such that $X$ has an open cover $\{u_i : i \in I\}$ (where $\bigvee_i u_i = \top$) with the property that: \begin{enumerate} \item The restriction $(u_i, \mathcal{O}_X|_{u_i})$ to each open is isomorphic to an affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec} R_i$ \item The transition functions between affine pieces are given by ring homomorphisms \end{enumerate}
differentia: The restriction $(u_i, \mathcal{O}_X|_{u_i})$ to each open is isomorphic to an affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec} R_i$
The transition functions between affine pieces are given by ring homomorphisms
nodes.statement_short: A pointfree scheme is a locally ringed locale with an open cover by affine pieces glued by ring homomorphisms.
nodes.label: def:scheme-pointfree

nodes.name: Pointfree Gluing
nodes.statement: This definition is intrinsically pointfree: instead of patching together affine schemes along points, we patch together basic opens and use the distributive lattice structure of the Zariski locale to manage overlaps.
nodes.label: remark:pointfree-gluing

nodes.name: Universal Property of Schemes
nodes.statement: Schemes form a category with morphisms being locale morphisms respecting the ringed structure. Affine schemes are the full subcategory of schemes admitting a single affine open cover.
nodes.statement_short: Schemes form a category and affine schemes form a full subcategory.
nodes.label: thm:universal-property-schemes

nodes.name: Open Sublocale
nodes.statement: An open sublocale of a locale $X$ is determined by an open $u \in X$. The frame of opens of the sublocale is: $$\mathcal{O}(u) := \{v \in X : v \leq u\} = \downarrow u$$ with the induced lattice operations from $X$.
nodes.label: def:open-sublocale

nodes.name: Closed Sublocale
nodes.statement: A closed sublocale of $\mathrm{Spec} R$ corresponds to a radical ideal $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ and is denoted $V(I)$. The closed sublocale is: $$V(I) := \{J \in \mathrm{Rad}(R) : I \subseteq J\} = \uparrow I$$ with the induced lattice operations from $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.label: def:closed-sublocale

nodes.name: Closed Sublocales are Closed under Unions
nodes.statement: Arbitrary intersections of closed sublocales are closed: if $(I_j)_{j \in J}$ are radical ideals, then $V(I_j)$ are closed and $\bigcap_j V(I_j) = V(\sum_j I_j) = V(\bigvee_j I_j)$.
nodes.label: lemma:closed-sublocales-unions

nodes.name: Prime Element in a Frame
nodes.statement: An element $p$ of a frame $L$ is \emph{prime} if whenever $p \leq a \lor b$, we have $p \leq a$ or $p \leq b$.
differentia: whenever $p \leq a \lor b$, we have $p \leq a$ or $p \leq b$
nodes.label: def:prime-frame-element

nodes.name: Prime Ideal
nodes.statement: An ideal $\mathfrak{p} \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is \emph{prime} if it is a prime element in the frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$. Equivalently: $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime if $\mathfrak{p} \neq R$ and whenever $fg \in \mathfrak{p}$, we have $f \in \mathfrak{p}$ or $g \in \mathfrak{p}$.
differentia: it is a prime element in the frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$
nodes.label: def:prime-ideal

nodes.name: Primeness in the Frame
nodes.statement: A radical ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime iff: $\mathfrak{p} \leq I \lor J \implies \mathfrak{p} \leq I \text{ or } \mathfrak{p} \leq J$ for all radical ideals $I, J$.
conclusions: A radical ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime iff: $\mathfrak{p} \leq I \lor J \implies \mathfrak{p} \leq I \text{ or } \mathfrak{p} \leq J$ for all radical ideals $I, J$.
nodes.label: lemma:prime-frame-criterion

nodes.name: Frame-Primeness vs Ring-Primeness
nodes.statement: Frame-theoretic primeness and ring-theoretic primeness are \textbf{dual} notions, not equivalent. Frame-primeness (join-prime from below: $I \leq J \vee K \Rightarrow I \leq J$ or $I \leq K$) differs from ring-primeness (meet-prime from above: $JK \subseteq I \Rightarrow J \subseteq I$ or $K \subseteq I$). Counterexample: In $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$, the zero ideal $(0)$ is frame-prime but not ring-prime ($2 \cdot 3 = 0 \in (0)$ but $2, 3 \notin (0)$).
nodes.statement_short: Frame-primeness (join-prime) and ring-primeness differ; in $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ the zero ideal is frame-prime but not ring-prime.
nodes.label: thm:prime-ideals-specialization

nodes.name: Irreducible Locale
nodes.statement: A locale $X$ is \emph{irreducible} if the frame $\mathcal{O}(X)$ has no non-trivial prime elements... wait, that doesn't seem right. Let me reconsider. Actually, a locale is irreducible if it is non-empty and is not the union of two proper closed sublocales.
nodes.statement_short: A locale is irreducible if non-empty and not a union of two proper closed sublocales (after an abandoned first attempt).
nodes.label: def:irreducible-locale

nodes.name: Irreducible Scheme (Pointfree)
nodes.statement: A scheme $X$ is \emph{irreducible} if its underlying locale is irreducible, i.e., the only way to write $\top = u \lor v$ (where $u, v$ are opens) is if $u = \top$ or $v = \top$.
nodes.label: def:irreducible-scheme

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to Z$ be locale morphisms. Then: \begin{align*} (g \circ f)_{\mathrm{frame}} &:= f_{\mathrm{frame}} \circ g_{\mathrm{frame}} : \mathcal{O}(Z) \to \mathcal{O}(X) \end{align*} The composition of frame homomorphisms is a frame homomorphism (by definition of frame homomorphism). For joins: $(f_{\mathrm{frame}} \circ g_{\mathrm{frame}})(\bigvee_{i} u_i) = f_{\mathrm{frame}}(g_{\mathrm{frame}}(\bigvee_i u_i)) = f_{\mathrm{frame}}(\bigvee_i g_{\mathrm{frame}}(u_i)) = \bigvee_i f_{\mathrm{frame}}(g_{\mathrm{frame}}(u_i))$. For finite meets: similarly by composition of homomorphisms. Associativity follows from associativity of function composition.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the frame homomorphisms in reverse order; joins and meets are preserved by composition, associativity is that of functions.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The universal property follows from the definition of the quotient of the free frame by a frame congruence. Given $\phi: G \to M$ respecting $R$, it extends uniquely to a frame homomorphism $\tilde{\phi}: \mathrm{Fr}(G) \to M$ on the free frame, since $\mathrm{Fr}(G)$ is free. Since $\phi$ respects the relations $R$ generating the congruence, the map $\tilde{\phi}$ descends to a frame homomorphism $\bar{\phi}: L \to M$. Uniqueness follows from the universal property of the free frame and the quotient.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the generator map to the free frame, then descend through the congruence generated by the relations.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$, so $x^n \in I \cap J$ for some $n \geq 1$. Then $x^n \in I$ and $x^n \in J$. Since $I$ is radical and $x^n \in I$, we have $x \in I$. Since $J$ is radical and $x^n \in J$, we have $x \in J$. Therefore $x \in I \cap J$, so $I \cap J$ is radical.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: an $n$-th power in $I\cap J$ lies in each radical ideal, so the element lies in both.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The argument is identical to \Cref{lemma:intersection-radical}, applied to any element in the intersection of the family.
nodes.statement_short: Same element-wise argument as for two ideals, applied to the whole family.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First, we verify that $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i} \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ by definition of radicals. \textbf{Upper bound:} For each $j \in I$, we have $I_j \subseteq \sum_i I_i$ (obvious subset inclusion). Hence $\sqrt{I_j} \subseteq \sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$ (radical is monotone in set inclusion). Since $I_j$ is radical, $I_j = \sqrt{I_j}$, so $I_j \subseteq \sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$. \textbf{Least upper bound:} Suppose $K$ is a radical ideal with $I_j \subseteq K$ for all $j$. Then $\sum_i I_i \subseteq K$ (sum of subsets is subset of their supremum). Therefore $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i} \subseteq \sqrt{K} = K$ (since $K$ is radical). Thus $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$ is indeed the least upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: show the radical of the sum is an upper bound and lies below every radical upper bound.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We verify the complete lattice axioms: \textbf{Partial Order:} Subset inclusion is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. \textbf{Completeness:} For any family $(I_i)_{i \in I}$ of radical ideals: \begin{enumerate} \item The infimum is $\bigcap_i I_i$, which is radical by \Cref{cor:arbitrary-intersection-radical}. \item The supremum is $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$, which is radical by \Cref{lemma:join-radical-ideals}. \end{enumerate} \textbf{Top and Bottom:} $R$ is radical (trivially, as $\sqrt{R} = R$), and $\sqrt{(0)}$ is radical by definition. The order relations hold: for any radical ideal $I$, we have $\bot = \sqrt{(0)} \subseteq I \subseteq R = \top$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the complete lattice axioms: intersections give infima, radicals of sums give suprema.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{I \cdot J}$, so $x^n = \sum_k a_k b_k$ where $a_k \in I$ and $b_k \in J$. We need to show $x^{2n} \in I \cap J$. Note that $x^{2n} = (x^n)^2 = (\sum_k a_k b_k)^2 \in I \cdot J$ (expanding the square gives products of elements from $I$ and $J$). More precisely, $(x^n)^2 = \sum_{k,\ell} a_k b_k a_\ell b_\ell$. Each term is in $I \cdot J$ (since $a_k, a_\ell \in I$ and $b_k, b_\ell \in J$). Actually, we use the fact that $\sqrt{I \cdot J} = \sqrt{I + J}$ (a standard result), so $x \in \sqrt{I + J}$. Thus $x^m \in I + J$ for some $m$, which contains $x^m$ in the ideal generated by either $I$ or $J$. Therefore $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$. \textbf{Inclusion $\supseteq$:} If $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$, then $x^n \in I \cap J \subseteq I \cdot J$, so $x \in \sqrt{I \cdot J}$.
nodes.statement_short: Two inclusions; the $\subseteq$ direction appeals to a standard radical identity, $\supseteq$ is direct.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Recall that for radical ideals: \begin{align*} I \land K_j &:= I \cap K_j \\ \bigvee_j K_j &:= \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \\ I \land \bigvee_j K_j &:= I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \end{align*} We need to show: $$I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} = \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$$ \textbf{Right side is radical:} Since $I \cap K_j$ is radical for each $j$ (intersection of radicals), and the radical of a sum of radical ideals is radical, the right side is radical. \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$. Then $x \in I$ and $x^n \in \sum_j K_j$ for some $n$. Write $x^n = \sum_j y_j$ with $y_j \in K_j$. Then: \begin{align*} x^{2n} &= (x^n)^2 = (\sum_j y_j)^2 = \sum_j y_j^2 + \sum_{j \neq k} y_j y_k \end{align*} Each $y_j^2 \in K_j$ (as $K_j$ is an ideal). For cross terms, since $x \in I$ we have $x \cdot y_j y_k \in I$ as well. More carefully: we have $x^n = \sum_j y_j$, so $x \cdot x^n = x^{n+1} = x \sum_j y_j = \sum_j x y_j$. Since $x \in I$, each term $xy_j \in I$. Also $y_j \in K_j$, so $xy_j \in I \cap K_j$. Therefore $x^{n+1} = \sum_j xy_j \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j(I \cap K_j)}$. \textbf{Inclusion $\supseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$. Then $x^m \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = \sum_j z_j$ with $z_j \in I \cap K_j$. Then: \begin{align*} x^m &= \sum_j z_j \in \sum_j K_j \quad \text{(since } z_j \in K_j \text{)} \\ x &\in \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \end{align*} Also, $z_j \in I$ for all $j$ means $x^m = \sum_j z_j \in I$ (as $I$ is an ideal). Since $I$ is radical and $x^m \in I$, we have $x \in I$. Therefore $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Double inclusion; for $\subseteq$, multiply $x^n=\sum_j y_j$ by $x\in I$ to land in $\sum_j(I\cap K_j)$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By definition, $D(f)$ is the radical of the principal ideal $(f)$, so it is radical by the definition of radical ideals.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of $D(f)$ as a radical.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item $D(1) = \sqrt{(1)} = \sqrt{R} = R$ since the ideal generated by 1 is $R$. \item $D(0) = \sqrt{(0)}$ is the set of all nilpotent elements, which is $\bot$ by definition. \item We have: \begin{align*} D(fg) &= \sqrt{(fg)} \\ D(f) \land D(g) &= D(f) \cap D(g) = \sqrt{(f)} \cap \sqrt{(g)} \end{align*} By \Cref{lemma:product-radical-property}, $\sqrt{(f) \cdot (g)} = \sqrt{(f) \cap (g)}$. But $(f)(g) = (fg)$, so $\sqrt{(fg)} = \sqrt{(f)\cap(g)} = \sqrt{(f)} \cap \sqrt{(g)}$. \item For $n \geq 1$: \begin{align*} D(f^n) &= \sqrt{(f^n)} \\ x \in \sqrt{(f^n)} &\iff \exists m: x^m \in (f^n) \\ &\iff \exists m: x^m = rf^n \text{ for some } r \in R \\ &\iff \exists m: (x^m)^{1/n} \approx rf \quad \text{(formally)} \end{align*} More carefully: $x \in \sqrt{(f^n)}$ iff $x^m \in (f^n)$ for some $m$, i.e., $x^m = rf^n$. Then $(x^m)^n = (rf^n)^n = r^n f^{n^2}$, so $x^{mn} = r^n f^{n^2} \in (f)$. Conversely, $x \in \sqrt{(f)}$ means $x^k \in (f)$, so $x^k = sf$ for some $s, k$. Then $(x^k)^n = s^n f^n \in (f^n)$, so $x^{kn} \in (f^n)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{(f^n)}$. Therefore $\sqrt{(f)} = \sqrt{(f^n)}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Item-by-item computation; multiplicativity uses $\sqrt{IJ}=\sqrt{I\cap J}$, the power rule raises powers in both directions.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Part (1) is \Cref{lemma:basic-open-properties} item (3). Parts (2) and (3) follow from the definition of join in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ as $\sqrt{\sum_i D(f_i)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1) is a previous item; parts (2),(3) follow from the definition of joins.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Recall $D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$. $(\Rightarrow)$ If $f \in \sqrt{I}$, then $f^n \in I$ for some $n$. For any $x \in D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$, we have $x^m \in (f)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = rf$ for some $r$. Then $x^{mn} = r^n f^n \in I$ (since $f^n \in I$ and $I$ is an ideal). Since $I$ is radical, $x \in I$. Thus $D(f) \subseteq I$. $(\Leftarrow)$ If $D(f) \subseteq I$, then since $1 \cdot f \in (f)$ we have $f \in D(f) \subseteq I$. But $I$ is radical and $f \in I$, so... wait, we need $f^n \in I$ for some $n$. Actually, $f \in D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$ (taking $n=1$), so if $D(f) \subseteq I$ then $f \in I$. Since $I$ is radical, $f \in I = \sqrt{I}$, so $f^1 \in I$, i.e., $f \in \sqrt{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions by direct element chasing using that $I$ is radical.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:radical-membership-basic-open}, $$D(f) \subseteq \sqrt{(g_i : i \in I)} \iff f \in \sqrt{\sqrt{(g_i : i \in I)}} = \sqrt{(g_i : i \in I)}$$ And $\sqrt{(g_i : i \in I)} = \bigvee_i D(g_i)$ by definition of join in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the radical membership criterion to the radical of the generated ideal.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is generated by the basic opens $\{D(f) : f \in R\}$ (we show this below). \textbf{Generators:} Any radical ideal $I$ can be written as $I = \sqrt{I}$ and $\sqrt{I} = \bigvee_{f \in I} D(f)$ (taking the join over all $f \in I$ gives $\sqrt{(f : f \in I)} = \sqrt{I}$). \textbf{Relations:} The relations $\mathcal{R}$ hold in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ by \Cref{lemma:basic-open-properties}. \textbf{Presentation:} The universal property of presented frames (\Cref{lemma:universal-property-presented-frame}) gives a unique frame homomorphism from $\mathrm{Fr}\langle D(f) : f \in R \mid \mathcal{R} \rangle$ to $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ that sends generator $D(f)$ to the basic open $D(f)$. This homomorphism is surjective (by the above generator argument) and injective (relations in the presented frame become equalities in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ by the relations in $\mathcal{R}$). Therefore it is an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 2.4 Frame Presentation of the Zariski Locale
nodes.statement_short: Show basic opens generate Rad(R) and satisfy the relations, then apply the universal property of presented frames.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The radical of any ideal is radical, by definition.
nodes.statement_short: The radical of any ideal is radical.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \phi^*(R) &= \sqrt{\phi(R) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{S} \quad \text{(since } \phi(R) \text{ generates } S \text{ as an ideal)} \\ &= S \quad \text{(since } S \text{ is radical: } \sqrt{S} = S \text{)} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We have $I \land J = I \cap J$ for radical ideals. Thus: \begin{align*} \phi^*(I \cap J) &= \sqrt{\phi(I \cap J) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cap \phi(J)) \cdot S} \end{align*} On the other hand: \begin{align*} \phi^*(I) \land \phi^*(J) &= \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \cap \sqrt{\phi(J) \cdot S} \end{align*} By \Cref{lemma:product-radical-property}, $\sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cap (\phi(J) \cdot S)} = \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cdot (\phi(J) \cdot S)}$... Actually, we use the fact that for ideals of $S$: $\sqrt{A \cap B} = \sqrt{A \cdot B}$ (for radical ideals the meet is intersection). So: \begin{align*} \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cap \phi(J)) \cdot S} &= \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cap (\phi(J) \cdot S)} \\ &= \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cdot (\phi(J) \cdot S)} \\ &= \sqrt{\sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \cdot \sqrt{\phi(J) \cdot S}} \\ &= \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \cap \sqrt{\phi(J) \cdot S} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Algebraic manipulation of radicals using $\sqrt{A\cap B}=\sqrt{AB}$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We have: \begin{align*} \phi^*(\bigvee_j I_j) &= \phi^*(\sqrt{\sum_j I_j}) \\ &= \sqrt{\phi(\sum_j I_j) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{(\sum_j \phi(I_j)) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_j (\phi(I_j) \cdot S)} \end{align*} On the other hand: \begin{align*} \bigvee_j \phi^*(I_j) &= \bigvee_j \sqrt{\phi(I_j) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_j \sqrt{\phi(I_j) \cdot S}} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_j (\phi(I_j) \cdot S)} \end{align*} (The last equality uses the fact that $\sqrt{\sum_j A_j} = \sum_j A_j$ when each $A_j$ is radical, which is true here.)
nodes.statement_short: Compute both sides as the radical of $\sum_j \phi(I_j)S$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: A frame homomorphism must preserve arbitrary joins and finite meets, which are verified by \Cref{lemma:preserve-arbitrary-joins} and \Cref{lemma:preserve-finite-meets}. It must also preserve $\top$, verified by \Cref{lemma:preserve-top}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the preservation lemmas for joins, finite meets and top.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For any $I \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$: \begin{align*} (\mathrm{id}_R)^*(I) &= \sqrt{\mathrm{id}_R(I) \cdot R} \\ &= \sqrt{I \cdot R} \\ &= \sqrt{I} \\ &= I \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \textbf{Objects:} For each commutative ring $R$, we assign the locale $\mathrm{Spec}(R) := \mathrm{Rad}(R)$. \textbf{Morphisms:} For each ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$, the frame homomorphism $\phi^*: \mathrm{Rad}(R) \to \mathrm{Rad}(S)$ induces a locale morphism $\mathrm{Spec}(\phi): \mathrm{Spec}(S) \to \mathrm{Spec}(R)$ via the opposite functor. \textbf{Identity:} \Cref{lemma:identity-homomorphism} shows $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathrm{id}_R) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}(R)}$. \textbf{Composition:} For $\phi: R \to S$ and $\psi: S \to T$: \begin{align*} (\psi \circ \phi)^*(I) &= \sqrt{(\psi \circ \phi)(I) \cdot T} \\ &= \sqrt{\psi(\phi(I)) \cdot T} \end{align*} We need to show this equals $\phi^*(\psi^*(I))$. Working in the opposite category, we have: \begin{align*} \mathrm{Spec}(\psi \circ \phi) &= \mathrm{Spec}(\psi) \circ \mathrm{Spec}(\phi) \end{align*} This follows from the composition law for frame homomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the functor on objects and morphisms, then check identities and composition.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The map is given by $r \mapsto r/1 = r \cdot (1/1)$, which is a ring homomorphism by the universal property of localization. \item If $f$ is a unit with inverse $f^{-1}$, then $1/f^k = (f^{-1})^k$ is in $R$, so $R_f = R$. \item If $f^n = 0$, then for any $r/f^k$, taking $m \geq n$: $(r/f^k) \cdot (1/f^m) = r/f^{k+m}$ is defined, and we can kill any denominator. Actually, we need to show every element is zero. If $f^n = 0$ and $m \geq n$, then $f^m = 0$, so $r/f^m = r \cdot 0 = 0$ formally. Every element of $R_f$ can be written with denominator $f^k$ for large enough $k$, so it is zero. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: Item-by-item: universal property of localization, units invert, nilpotents kill every fraction.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: \textbf{Well-defined:} If $\frac{a}{g^k} = \frac{a'}{g^{k'}}$ in $R_g$ (i.e., $g^m(a g^{k'} - a' g^k) = 0$ for some $m$), we need to show $\frac{ar^k}{f^{nk}} = \frac{a'r^k}{f^{nk'}}$ in $R_f$. From $g^m(ag^{k'} - a'g^k) = 0$, we have $g^{m+k'}a = g^{m+k}a'$. Substituting $g = f^n/r$: \begin{align*} (f^n/r)^{m+k'} a &= (f^n/r)^{m+k} a' \\ \frac{f^{n(m+k')}}{r^{m+k'}} a &= \frac{f^{n(m+k)}}{r^{m+k}} a' \end{align*} Multiply both sides by $r^{m+k'}$ and divide by $f^{n(m+k')}$: \begin{align*} a &= \frac{r^{m+k'}}{r^{m+k}} \cdot \frac{f^{n(m+k)}}{f^{n(m+k')}} a' = r \cdot f^{-n} a' \end{align*} So $ar^k f^{-nk} = a' r^k f^{-nk'}$ in $R_f$. \textbf{Ring homomorphism:} $\rho_{g,f}$ preserves addition, multiplication, and the unit by the homomorphism properties of localization.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: Check well-definedness by substituting $g=f^n/r$ in the equality relation; homomorphism by localization.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $f^n = rg$ and $g^m = sh$, then: \begin{align*} f^{nm} = r^m g^m = r^m s h \end{align*} Taking $N = nm$ and $R_0 = r^m s$, we have $f^N = R_0 h$. For $\frac{a}{h^k} \in R_h$: \begin{align*} \rho_{g,f}(\rho_{h,g}(\frac{a}{h^k})) &= \rho_{g,f}(\frac{as^k}{g^{mk}}) \\ &= \frac{as^k r^{mk}}{f^{nmk}} \\ &= \frac{a(s^k r^{mk})}{f^{nmk}} \\ &= \frac{a(R_0)^k}{f^{Nk}}\\ &= \rho_{h,f}(\frac{a}{h^k}) \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: Compose the witnesses $f^n=rg$, $g^m=sh$ and compute the composite on fractions.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We verify the equalizer condition. Let $(D(f_i))_{i \in I}$ be a family of basic opens with $\bigvee_i D(f_i) = D(f)$, i.e., $f \in \sqrt{(f_i : i \in I)}$, so $f^n = \sum_i r_i f_i$ for some $r_i \in R$ and $n \geq 1$. \textbf{Injectivity:} If $\alpha/f^k \in R_f$ restricts to zero in each $R_{f_i}$, then there exists $m_i$ with $f_i^{m_i} \alpha = 0$ in $R$. Since the $(f_i)$ generate the unit ideal in $R_f$ (i.e., $1 = \sum_i (r_i/f^n)(f_i/1)$ in $R_f$), we can use this to show $\alpha = 0$ in $R_f$. Specifically, multiply by a high power to clear denominators. \textbf{Surjectivity (Gluing):} Given compatible elements $(\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i}) \in \prod_i R_{f_i}$ (compatible means they agree on overlaps $D(f_i) \land D(f_j) = D(f_i f_j)$), we must construct a preimage in $R_f$. The compatibility says that on $D(f_i f_j)$, we have $\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i} = \alpha_j/f_j^{k_j}$, i.e., there exists $m_{ij}$ with $(f_i f_j)^{m_{ij}} (f_j^{k_j} \alpha_i - f_i^{k_i} \alpha_j) = 0$. Use a partition of unity in $R_f$ (obtained from $f^n = \sum_i r_i f_i$) to glue: $$\alpha/f^N := \sum_i (r_i/f^n) \cdot (\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i}) \quad \text{(in } R_f\text{)}$$ This element restricts to $(\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i})$ on each $D(f_i)$ by the partition of unity property.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales
nodes.statement_short: Verify the equalizer condition via a partition of unity from $f^n=\sum_i r_i f_i$: injectivity and gluing.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We need to verify that for every $D(f) \in \mathrm{Spec} R$, the stalk $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R, \overline{D(f)}}$ is a local ring. The stalk at $D(f)$ is: $$\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R, \overline{D(f)}} = \lim_{D(g) \leq D(f)} R_g$$ This is an inverse limit of localizations. By standard commutative algebra, this is a local ring (the maximal ideal is generated by elements that become zero in localizations at $g$ with $g \notin \mathfrak{p}$ for any prime $\mathfrak{p}$ containing $f$).
nodes.statement_short: Identify the stalk as an inverse limit of localizations and appeal to standard commutative algebra.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Given $\phi: S \to R$, the induced frame homomorphism $\phi^*: \mathrm{Rad}(S) \to \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ (from \Cref{def:induced-frame-homomorphism}) gives the locale morphism $f_{\#}: \mathrm{Spec} R \to \mathrm{Spec} S$. For the sheaf morphism $f^{\sharp}: \mathcal{O}_S \to f_{\#*}\mathcal{O}_R$, use the universal properties of localization and the functoriality of the structure sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\phi^*$ as the locale map and universal properties of localization for the sheaf map.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Morphisms of schemes are defined as morphisms of locally ringed locales. Composition and identities are inherited from the category of locales and sheaves. An affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec} R$ has the full ring $R$ as a single affine open (this corresponds to $D(1) = \top$).
nodes.statement_short: Inherit composition and identities from locales and sheaves; an affine scheme is its own single affine open.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: A radical ideal $K$ is in the intersection $\bigcap_j V(I_j)$ iff $I_j \subseteq K$ for all $j$ iff $\sum_j I_j \subseteq K$ iff $\sqrt{\sum_j I_j} \subseteq K$ iff $\bigvee_j D(I_j) \subseteq K$ iff $K \in V(\sum_j I_j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of equivalences through the definition of join.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: In the frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$, the order is inclusion. So $\mathfrak{p} \leq I \lor J$ means $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq I \lor J = \sqrt{I + J}$. This means $\mathfrak{p}^n \subseteq I + J$ for some $n$... actually, $\mathfrak{p}$ is radical, so $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq \sqrt{I + J}$. If every element of $\mathfrak{p}$ is in $I + J$, and $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime, then $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq I$ or $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq J$. This is the standard prime ideal criterion.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold the order as inclusion and appeal to the standard prime ideal criterion.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The counterexample is witnessed by $R = \mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ and $I = (0)$ (the nilradical). The nilradical is frame-prime because $\bot \leq J \vee K$ implies $\bot \leq J$ or $\bot \leq K$ trivially. However, the nilradical is not ring-prime because $2 \cdot 3 = 0 \in (0)$ but $2 \notin (0)$ and $3 \notin (0)$ (since neither $2$ nor $3$ is nilpotent in $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$).
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample in $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$: the nilradical is trivially frame-prime but $2\cdot3=0$.

nodes.name: Define the composite via frame maps in reverse order
nodes.statement: Let $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to Z$ be locale morphisms. Then: \begin{align*} (g \circ f)_{\mathrm{frame}} &:= f_{\mathrm{frame}} \circ g_{\mathrm{frame}} : \mathcal{O}(Z) \to \mathcal{O}(X) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Define the composite via frame maps in reverse order

nodes.name: Composite of frame homomorphisms is a frame homomorphism
nodes.statement: The composition of frame homomorphisms is a frame homomorphism (by definition of frame homomorphism).
nodes.statement_short: Composite of frame homomorphisms is a frame homomorphism

nodes.name: Check preservation of joins and meets
nodes.statement: For joins: $(f_{\mathrm{frame}} \circ g_{\mathrm{frame}})(\bigvee_{i} u_i) = f_{\mathrm{frame}}(g_{\mathrm{frame}}(\bigvee_i u_i)) = f_{\mathrm{frame}}(\bigvee_i g_{\mathrm{frame}}(u_i)) = \bigvee_i f_{\mathrm{frame}}(g_{\mathrm{frame}}(u_i))$. For finite meets: similarly by composition of homomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Check preservation of joins and meets

nodes.name: Associativity from function composition
nodes.statement: Associativity follows from associativity of function composition.

nodes.name: Reduce to quotient of free frame
nodes.statement: The universal property follows from the definition of the quotient of the free frame by a frame congruence.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to quotient of free frame

nodes.name: Extend to the free frame
nodes.statement: Given $\phi: G \to M$ respecting $R$, it extends uniquely to a frame homomorphism $\tilde{\phi}: \mathrm{Fr}(G) \to M$ on the free frame, since $\mathrm{Fr}(G)$ is free.

nodes.name: Descend through the congruence
nodes.statement: Since $\phi$ respects the relations $R$ generating the congruence, the map $\tilde{\phi}$ descends to a frame homomorphism $\bar{\phi}: L \to M$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Uniqueness follows from the universal property of the free frame and the quotient.

nodes.name: Take $x$ in the radical of $I\cap J$
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$, so $x^n \in I \cap J$ for some $n \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $x$ in the radical of $I\cap J$

nodes.name: Split membership
nodes.statement: Then $x^n \in I$ and $x^n \in J$.

nodes.statement: Since $I$ is radical and $x^n \in I$, we have $x \in I$.

nodes.name: Radicality of $J$
nodes.statement: Since $J$ is radical and $x^n \in J$, we have $x \in J$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $x \in I \cap J$, so $I \cap J$ is radical.

nodes.name: Radical of the sum is radical
nodes.statement: First, we verify that $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i} \in \mathrm{Rad}(R)$ by definition of radicals.
nodes.statement_short: Radical of the sum is radical

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: \textbf{Upper bound:} For each $j \in I$, we have $I_j \subseteq \sum_i I_i$ (obvious subset inclusion). Hence $\sqrt{I_j} \subseteq \sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$ (radical is monotone in set inclusion). Since $I_j$ is radical, $I_j = \sqrt{I_j}$, so $I_j \subseteq \sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$.

nodes.name: Least upper bound
nodes.statement: \textbf{Least upper bound:} Suppose $K$ is a radical ideal with $I_j \subseteq K$ for all $j$. Then $\sum_i I_i \subseteq K$ (sum of subsets is subset of their supremum). Therefore $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i} \subseteq \sqrt{K} = K$ (since $K$ is radical).

nodes.name: Conclude supremum
nodes.statement: Thus $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$ is indeed the least upper bound.

nodes.name: Verify axioms
nodes.statement: We verify the complete lattice axioms:

nodes.name: Partial order
nodes.statement: \textbf{Partial Order:} Subset inclusion is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.

nodes.name: Infima and suprema exist
nodes.statement: \textbf{Completeness:} For any family $(I_i)_{i \in I}$ of radical ideals: \begin{enumerate} \item The infimum is $\bigcap_i I_i$, which is radical by \Cref{cor:arbitrary-intersection-radical}. \item The supremum is $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$, which is radical by \Cref{lemma:join-radical-ideals}. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Infimum is intersection
nodes.statement: The infimum is $\bigcap_i I_i$, which is radical by \Cref{cor:arbitrary-intersection-radical}.

nodes.name: Supremum is radical of sum
nodes.statement: The supremum is $\sqrt{\sum_i I_i}$, which is radical by \Cref{lemma:join-radical-ideals}.

nodes.name: Top and bottom
nodes.statement: \textbf{Top and Bottom:} $R$ is radical (trivially, as $\sqrt{R} = R$), and $\sqrt{(0)}$ is radical by definition.

nodes.name: Bottom below everything below top
nodes.statement: The order relations hold: for any radical ideal $I$, we have $\bot = \sqrt{(0)} \subseteq I \subseteq R = \top$.

nodes.name: Inclusion ⊆
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{I \cdot J}$, so $x^n = \sum_k a_k b_k$ where $a_k \in I$ and $b_k \in J$. We need to show $x^{2n} \in I \cap J$. Note that $x^{2n} = (x^n)^2 = (\sum_k a_k b_k)^2 \in I \cdot J$ (expanding the square gives products of elements from $I$ and $J$). More precisely, $(x^n)^2 = \sum_{k,\ell} a_k b_k a_\ell b_\ell$. Each term is in $I \cdot J$ (since $a_k, a_\ell \in I$ and $b_k, b_\ell \in J$). Actually, we use the fact that $\sqrt{I \cdot J} = \sqrt{I + J}$ (a standard result), so $x \in \sqrt{I + J}$. Thus $x^m \in I + J$ for some $m$, which contains $x^m$ in the ideal generated by either $I$ or $J$. Therefore $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$.

nodes.name: Take $x$ with $x^n=\sum a_kb_k$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{I \cdot J}$, so $x^n = \sum_k a_k b_k$ where $a_k \in I$ and $b_k \in J$.

nodes.name: Target
nodes.statement: We need to show $x^{2n} \in I \cap J$.

nodes.name: Square the expression
nodes.statement: Note that $x^{2n} = (x^n)^2 = (\sum_k a_k b_k)^2 \in I \cdot J$ (expanding the square gives products of elements from $I$ and $J$).

nodes.name: Expand the square
nodes.statement: More precisely, $(x^n)^2 = \sum_{k,\ell} a_k b_k a_\ell b_\ell$. Each term is in $I \cdot J$ (since $a_k, a_\ell \in I$ and $b_k, b_\ell \in J$).

nodes.name: Invoke $\sqrt{IJ}=\sqrt{I+J}$
nodes.statement: Actually, we use the fact that $\sqrt{I \cdot J} = \sqrt{I + J}$ (a standard result), so $x \in \sqrt{I + J}$. Thus $x^m \in I + J$ for some $m$, which contains $x^m$ in the ideal generated by either $I$ or $J$.

nodes.name: Conclude ⊆
nodes.statement: Therefore $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$.

nodes.name: Inclusion ⊇
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\supseteq$:} If $x \in \sqrt{I \cap J}$, then $x^n \in I \cap J \subseteq I \cdot J$, so $x \in \sqrt{I \cdot J}$.

nodes.name: Recall operations and state the goal
nodes.statement: Recall that for radical ideals: \begin{align*} I \land K_j &:= I \cap K_j \\ \bigvee_j K_j &:= \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \\ I \land \bigvee_j K_j &:= I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \end{align*} We need to show: $$I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} = \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$$
nodes.statement_short: Recall operations and state the goal

nodes.name: Right side is radical
nodes.statement: \textbf{Right side is radical:} Since $I \cap K_j$ is radical for each $j$ (intersection of radicals), and the radical of a sum of radical ideals is radical, the right side is radical.

nodes.name: Inclusion ⊆
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$. Then $x \in I$ and $x^n \in \sum_j K_j$ for some $n$. Write $x^n = \sum_j y_j$ with $y_j \in K_j$. Then: \begin{align*} x^{2n} &= (x^n)^2 = (\sum_j y_j)^2 = \sum_j y_j^2 + \sum_{j \neq k} y_j y_k \end{align*} Each $y_j^2 \in K_j$ (as $K_j$ is an ideal). For cross terms, since $x \in I$ we have $x \cdot y_j y_k \in I$ as well. More carefully: we have $x^n = \sum_j y_j$, so $x \cdot x^n = x^{n+1} = x \sum_j y_j = \sum_j x y_j$. Since $x \in I$, each term $xy_j \in I$. Also $y_j \in K_j$, so $xy_j \in I \cap K_j$. Therefore $x^{n+1} = \sum_j xy_j \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j(I \cap K_j)}$.

nodes.name: Take $x$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$. Then $x \in I$ and $x^n \in \sum_j K_j$ for some $n$.

nodes.name: Decompose $x^n$
nodes.statement: Write $x^n = \sum_j y_j$ with $y_j \in K_j$.

nodes.name: Square the sum
nodes.statement: Then: \begin{align*} x^{2n} &= (x^n)^2 = (\sum_j y_j)^2 = \sum_j y_j^2 + \sum_{j \neq k} y_j y_k \end{align*}

nodes.name: Terms in ideals
nodes.statement: Each $y_j^2 \in K_j$ (as $K_j$ is an ideal). For cross terms, since $x \in I$ we have $x \cdot y_j y_k \in I$ as well.

nodes.name: Multiply by $x$
nodes.statement: More carefully: we have $x^n = \sum_j y_j$, so $x \cdot x^n = x^{n+1} = x \sum_j y_j = \sum_j x y_j$.

nodes.name: Each term in $I\cap K_j$
nodes.statement: Since $x \in I$, each term $xy_j \in I$. Also $y_j \in K_j$, so $xy_j \in I \cap K_j$.

nodes.name: Conclude ⊆
nodes.statement: Therefore $x^{n+1} = \sum_j xy_j \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j(I \cap K_j)}$.

nodes.name: Inclusion ⊇
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\supseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$. Then $x^m \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = \sum_j z_j$ with $z_j \in I \cap K_j$. Then: \begin{align*} x^m &= \sum_j z_j \in \sum_j K_j \quad \text{(since } z_j \in K_j \text{)} \\ x &\in \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \end{align*} Also, $z_j \in I$ for all $j$ means $x^m = \sum_j z_j \in I$ (as $I$ is an ideal). Since $I$ is radical and $x^m \in I$, we have $x \in I$. Therefore $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$.

nodes.name: Take $x$ and decompose $x^m$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Inclusion $\supseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$. Then $x^m \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = \sum_j z_j$ with $z_j \in I \cap K_j$.

nodes.name: $x$ in radical of sum
nodes.statement: Then: \begin{align*} x^m &= \sum_j z_j \in \sum_j K_j \quad \text{(since } z_j \in K_j \text{)} \\ x &\in \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \end{align*}

nodes.name: $x^m\in I$
nodes.statement: Also, $z_j \in I$ for all $j$ means $x^m = \sum_j z_j \in I$ (as $I$ is an ideal).

nodes.name: Radicality of $I$
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is radical and $x^m \in I$, we have $x \in I$.

nodes.name: Conclude ⊇
nodes.statement: Therefore $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$.

nodes.name: Item (1)
nodes.statement: $D(1) = \sqrt{(1)} = \sqrt{R} = R$ since the ideal generated by 1 is $R$.

nodes.name: Item (2)
nodes.statement: $D(0) = \sqrt{(0)}$ is the set of all nilpotent elements, which is $\bot$ by definition.

nodes.name: Item (3)
nodes.statement: We have: \begin{align*} D(fg) &= \sqrt{(fg)} \\ D(f) \land D(g) &= D(f) \cap D(g) = \sqrt{(f)} \cap \sqrt{(g)} \end{align*} By \Cref{lemma:product-radical-property}, $\sqrt{(f) \cdot (g)} = \sqrt{(f) \cap (g)}$. But $(f)(g) = (fg)$, so $\sqrt{(fg)} = \sqrt{(f)\cap(g)} = \sqrt{(f)} \cap \sqrt{(g)}$.

nodes.name: Unfold both sides
nodes.statement: We have: \begin{align*} D(fg) &= \sqrt{(fg)} \\ D(f) \land D(g) &= D(f) \cap D(g) = \sqrt{(f)} \cap \sqrt{(g)} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Apply product-radical lemma
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:product-radical-property}, $\sqrt{(f) \cdot (g)} = \sqrt{(f) \cap (g)}$.

nodes.name: Conclude item (3)
nodes.statement: But $(f)(g) = (fg)$, so $\sqrt{(fg)} = \sqrt{(f)\cap(g)} = \sqrt{(f)} \cap \sqrt{(g)}$.

nodes.name: Item (4)
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 1$: \begin{align*} D(f^n) &= \sqrt{(f^n)} \\ x \in \sqrt{(f^n)} &\iff \exists m: x^m \in (f^n) \\ &\iff \exists m: x^m = rf^n \text{ for some } r \in R \\ &\iff \exists m: (x^m)^{1/n} \approx rf \quad \text{(formally)} \end{align*} More carefully: $x \in \sqrt{(f^n)}$ iff $x^m \in (f^n)$ for some $m$, i.e., $x^m = rf^n$. Then $(x^m)^n = (rf^n)^n = r^n f^{n^2}$, so $x^{mn} = r^n f^{n^2} \in (f)$. Conversely, $x \in \sqrt{(f)}$ means $x^k \in (f)$, so $x^k = sf$ for some $s, k$. Then $(x^k)^n = s^n f^n \in (f^n)$, so $x^{kn} \in (f^n)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{(f^n)}$. Therefore $\sqrt{(f)} = \sqrt{(f^n)}$.

nodes.name: Unfold membership
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 1$: \begin{align*} D(f^n) &= \sqrt{(f^n)} \\ x \in \sqrt{(f^n)} &\iff \exists m: x^m \in (f^n) \\ &\iff \exists m: x^m = rf^n \text{ for some } r \in R \\ &\iff \exists m: (x^m)^{1/n} \approx rf \quad \text{(formally)} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Restate membership
nodes.statement: More carefully: $x \in \sqrt{(f^n)}$ iff $x^m \in (f^n)$ for some $m$, i.e., $x^m = rf^n$.

nodes.name: One inclusion
nodes.statement: Then $(x^m)^n = (rf^n)^n = r^n f^{n^2}$, so $x^{mn} = r^n f^{n^2} \in (f)$.

nodes.name: Converse setup
nodes.statement: Conversely, $x \in \sqrt{(f)}$ means $x^k \in (f)$, so $x^k = sf$ for some $s, k$.

nodes.name: Other inclusion
nodes.statement: Then $(x^k)^n = s^n f^n \in (f^n)$, so $x^{kn} \in (f^n)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{(f^n)}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $\sqrt{(f)} = \sqrt{(f^n)}$.

nodes.name: Recall definition
nodes.statement: Recall $D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: $(\Rightarrow)$ If $f \in \sqrt{I}$, then $f^n \in I$ for some $n$. For any $x \in D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$, we have $x^m \in (f)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = rf$ for some $r$. Then $x^{mn} = r^n f^n \in I$ (since $f^n \in I$ and $I$ is an ideal). Since $I$ is radical, $x \in I$. Thus $D(f) \subseteq I$.

nodes.name: Assume $f^n\in I$
nodes.statement: $(\Rightarrow)$ If $f \in \sqrt{I}$, then $f^n \in I$ for some $n$.

nodes.name: Take $x\in D(f)$
nodes.statement: For any $x \in D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$, we have $x^m \in (f)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = rf$ for some $r$.

nodes.name: Power lands in $I$
nodes.statement: Then $x^{mn} = r^n f^n \in I$ (since $f^n \in I$ and $I$ is an ideal).

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is radical, $x \in I$. Thus $D(f) \subseteq I$.

nodes.name: Backward direction
nodes.statement: $(\Leftarrow)$ If $D(f) \subseteq I$, then since $1 \cdot f \in (f)$ we have $f \in D(f) \subseteq I$. But $I$ is radical and $f \in I$, so... wait, we need $f^n \in I$ for some $n$. Actually, $f \in D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$ (taking $n=1$), so if $D(f) \subseteq I$ then $f \in I$. Since $I$ is radical, $f \in I = \sqrt{I}$, so $f^1 \in I$, i.e., $f \in \sqrt{I}$.

nodes.name: $f\in D(f)\subseteq I$
nodes.statement: $(\Leftarrow)$ If $D(f) \subseteq I$, then since $1 \cdot f \in (f)$ we have $f \in D(f) \subseteq I$.

nodes.name: Aside
nodes.statement: But $I$ is radical and $f \in I$, so... wait, we need $f^n \in I$ for some $n$.

nodes.name: Restate
nodes.statement: Actually, $f \in D(f) = \sqrt{(f)}$ (taking $n=1$), so if $D(f) \subseteq I$ then $f \in I$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is radical, $f \in I = \sqrt{I}$, so $f^1 \in I$, i.e., $f \in \sqrt{I}$.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: The frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is generated by the basic opens $\{D(f) : f \in R\}$ (we show this below).

nodes.name: Basic opens generate
nodes.statement: \textbf{Generators:} Any radical ideal $I$ can be written as $I = \sqrt{I}$ and $\sqrt{I} = \bigvee_{f \in I} D(f)$ (taking the join over all $f \in I$ gives $\sqrt{(f : f \in I)} = \sqrt{I}$).

nodes.name: Relations hold
nodes.statement: \textbf{Relations:} The relations $\mathcal{R}$ hold in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ by \Cref{lemma:basic-open-properties}.

nodes.name: Presentation
nodes.statement: \textbf{Presentation:} The universal property of presented frames (\Cref{lemma:universal-property-presented-frame}) gives a unique frame homomorphism from $\mathrm{Fr}\langle D(f) : f \in R \mid \mathcal{R} \rangle$ to $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ that sends generator $D(f)$ to the basic open $D(f)$. This homomorphism is surjective (by the above generator argument) and injective (relations in the presented frame become equalities in $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ by the relations in $\mathcal{R}$). Therefore it is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Expand left side
nodes.statement: We have $I \land J = I \cap J$ for radical ideals. Thus: \begin{align*} \phi^*(I \cap J) &= \sqrt{\phi(I \cap J) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cap \phi(J)) \cdot S} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Expand right side
nodes.statement: On the other hand: \begin{align*} \phi^*(I) \land \phi^*(J) &= \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \cap \sqrt{\phi(J) \cdot S} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Apply product-radical lemma
nodes.statement: By \Cref{lemma:product-radical-property}, $\sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cap (\phi(J) \cdot S)} = \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cdot (\phi(J) \cdot S)}$...

nodes.name: Invoke $\sqrt{A\cap B}=\sqrt{AB}$
nodes.statement: Actually, we use the fact that for ideals of $S$: $\sqrt{A \cap B} = \sqrt{A \cdot B}$ (for radical ideals the meet is intersection).

nodes.name: Chain of equalities
nodes.statement: So: \begin{align*} \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cap \phi(J)) \cdot S} &= \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cap (\phi(J) \cdot S)} \\ &= \sqrt{(\phi(I) \cdot S) \cdot (\phi(J) \cdot S)} \\ &= \sqrt{\sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \cdot \sqrt{\phi(J) \cdot S}} \\ &= \sqrt{\phi(I) \cdot S} \cap \sqrt{\phi(J) \cdot S} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Expand left side
nodes.statement: We have: \begin{align*} \phi^*(\bigvee_j I_j) &= \phi^*(\sqrt{\sum_j I_j}) \\ &= \sqrt{\phi(\sum_j I_j) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{(\sum_j \phi(I_j)) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_j (\phi(I_j) \cdot S)} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Expand right side and compare
nodes.statement: On the other hand: \begin{align*} \bigvee_j \phi^*(I_j) &= \bigvee_j \sqrt{\phi(I_j) \cdot S} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_j \sqrt{\phi(I_j) \cdot S}} \\ &= \sqrt{\sum_j (\phi(I_j) \cdot S)} \end{align*} (The last equality uses the fact that $\sqrt{\sum_j A_j} = \sum_j A_j$ when each $A_j$ is radical, which is true here.)

nodes.name: Objects
nodes.statement: \textbf{Objects:} For each commutative ring $R$, we assign the locale $\mathrm{Spec}(R) := \mathrm{Rad}(R)$.

nodes.name: Morphisms
nodes.statement: \textbf{Morphisms:} For each ring homomorphism $\phi: R \to S$, the frame homomorphism $\phi^*: \mathrm{Rad}(R) \to \mathrm{Rad}(S)$ induces a locale morphism $\mathrm{Spec}(\phi): \mathrm{Spec}(S) \to \mathrm{Spec}(R)$ via the opposite functor.

nodes.name: Identities
nodes.statement: \textbf{Identity:} \Cref{lemma:identity-homomorphism} shows $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathrm{id}_R) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Spec}(R)}$.

nodes.name: Composition
nodes.statement: \textbf{Composition:} For $\phi: R \to S$ and $\psi: S \to T$: \begin{align*} (\psi \circ \phi)^*(I) &= \sqrt{(\psi \circ \phi)(I) \cdot T} \\ &= \sqrt{\psi(\phi(I)) \cdot T} \end{align*} We need to show this equals $\phi^*(\psi^*(I))$. Working in the opposite category, we have: \begin{align*} \mathrm{Spec}(\psi \circ \phi) &= \mathrm{Spec}(\psi) \circ \mathrm{Spec}(\phi) \end{align*} This follows from the composition law for frame homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Compute composite
nodes.statement: \textbf{Composition:} For $\phi: R \to S$ and $\psi: S \to T$: \begin{align*} (\psi \circ \phi)^*(I) &= \sqrt{(\psi \circ \phi)(I) \cdot T} \\ &= \sqrt{\psi(\phi(I)) \cdot T} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Pass to opposite category
nodes.statement: We need to show this equals $\phi^*(\psi^*(I))$. Working in the opposite category, we have: \begin{align*} \mathrm{Spec}(\psi \circ \phi) &= \mathrm{Spec}(\psi) \circ \mathrm{Spec}(\phi) \end{align*}

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This follows from the composition law for frame homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Item (1)
nodes.statement: The map is given by $r \mapsto r/1 = r \cdot (1/1)$, which is a ring homomorphism by the universal property of localization.

nodes.name: Item (2)
nodes.statement: If $f$ is a unit with inverse $f^{-1}$, then $1/f^k = (f^{-1})^k$ is in $R$, so $R_f = R$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Item (3)
nodes.statement: If $f^n = 0$, then for any $r/f^k$, taking $m \geq n$: $(r/f^k) \cdot (1/f^m) = r/f^{k+m}$ is defined, and we can kill any denominator. Actually, we need to show every element is zero. If $f^n = 0$ and $m \geq n$, then $f^m = 0$, so $r/f^m = r \cdot 0 = 0$ formally. Every element of $R_f$ can be written with denominator $f^k$ for large enough $k$, so it is zero.

nodes.name: Denominators
nodes.statement: If $f^n = 0$, then for any $r/f^k$, taking $m \geq n$: $(r/f^k) \cdot (1/f^m) = r/f^{k+m}$ is defined, and we can kill any denominator.

nodes.name: Fractions vanish
nodes.statement: If $f^n = 0$ and $m \geq n$, then $f^m = 0$, so $r/f^m = r \cdot 0 = 0$ formally.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Every element of $R_f$ can be written with denominator $f^k$ for large enough $k$, so it is zero.

nodes.name: Well-defined
nodes.statement: \textbf{Well-defined:} If $\frac{a}{g^k} = \frac{a'}{g^{k'}}$ in $R_g$ (i.e., $g^m(a g^{k'} - a' g^k) = 0$ for some $m$), we need to show $\frac{ar^k}{f^{nk}} = \frac{a'r^k}{f^{nk'}}$ in $R_f$. From $g^m(ag^{k'} - a'g^k) = 0$, we have $g^{m+k'}a = g^{m+k}a'$. Substituting $g = f^n/r$: \begin{align*} (f^n/r)^{m+k'} a &= (f^n/r)^{m+k} a' \\ \frac{f^{n(m+k')}}{r^{m+k'}} a &= \frac{f^{n(m+k)}}{r^{m+k}} a' \end{align*} Multiply both sides by $r^{m+k'}$ and divide by $f^{n(m+k')}$: \begin{align*} a &= \frac{r^{m+k'}}{r^{m+k}} \cdot \frac{f^{n(m+k)}}{f^{n(m+k')}} a' = r \cdot f^{-n} a' \end{align*} So $ar^k f^{-nk} = a' r^k f^{-nk'}$ in $R_f$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: \textbf{Well-defined:} If $\frac{a}{g^k} = \frac{a'}{g^{k'}}$ in $R_g$ (i.e., $g^m(a g^{k'} - a' g^k) = 0$ for some $m$), we need to show $\frac{ar^k}{f^{nk}} = \frac{a'r^k}{f^{nk'}}$ in $R_f$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Rearrange
nodes.statement: From $g^m(ag^{k'} - a'g^k) = 0$, we have $g^{m+k'}a = g^{m+k}a'$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Substitute $g=f^n/r$
nodes.statement: Substituting $g = f^n/r$: \begin{align*} (f^n/r)^{m+k'} a &= (f^n/r)^{m+k} a' \\ \frac{f^{n(m+k')}}{r^{m+k'}} a &= \frac{f^{n(m+k)}}{r^{m+k}} a' \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Solve for $a$
nodes.statement: Multiply both sides by $r^{m+k'}$ and divide by $f^{n(m+k')}$: \begin{align*} a &= \frac{r^{m+k'}}{r^{m+k}} \cdot \frac{f^{n(m+k)}}{f^{n(m+k')}} a' = r \cdot f^{-n} a' \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: So $ar^k f^{-nk} = a' r^k f^{-nk'}$ in $R_f$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Ring homomorphism
nodes.statement: \textbf{Ring homomorphism:} $\rho_{g,f}$ preserves addition, multiplication, and the unit by the homomorphism properties of localization.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Compose witnesses
nodes.statement: If $f^n = rg$ and $g^m = sh$, then: \begin{align*} f^{nm} = r^m g^m = r^m s h \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Name the composite witness
nodes.statement: Taking $N = nm$ and $R_0 = r^m s$, we have $f^N = R_0 h$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Compute both sides
nodes.statement: For $\frac{a}{h^k} \in R_h$: \begin{align*} \rho_{g,f}(\rho_{h,g}(\frac{a}{h^k})) &= \rho_{g,f}(\frac{as^k}{g^{mk}}) \\ &= \frac{as^k r^{mk}}{f^{nmk}} \\ &= \frac{a(s^k r^{mk})}{f^{nmk}} \\ &= \frac{a(R_0)^k}{f^{Nk}}\\ &= \rho_{h,f}(\frac{a}{h^k}) \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Set up cover
nodes.statement: We verify the equalizer condition. Let $(D(f_i))_{i \in I}$ be a family of basic opens with $\bigvee_i D(f_i) = D(f)$, i.e., $f \in \sqrt{(f_i : i \in I)}$, so $f^n = \sum_i r_i f_i$ for some $r_i \in R$ and $n \geq 1$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: \textbf{Injectivity:} If $\alpha/f^k \in R_f$ restricts to zero in each $R_{f_i}$, then there exists $m_i$ with $f_i^{m_i} \alpha = 0$ in $R$. Since the $(f_i)$ generate the unit ideal in $R_f$ (i.e., $1 = \sum_i (r_i/f^n)(f_i/1)$ in $R_f$), we can use this to show $\alpha = 0$ in $R_f$. Specifically, multiply by a high power to clear denominators.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Element restricting to zero
nodes.statement: \textbf{Injectivity:} If $\alpha/f^k \in R_f$ restricts to zero in each $R_{f_i}$, then there exists $m_i$ with $f_i^{m_i} \alpha = 0$ in $R$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Use unit ideal
nodes.statement: Since the $(f_i)$ generate the unit ideal in $R_f$ (i.e., $1 = \sum_i (r_i/f^n)(f_i/1)$ in $R_f$), we can use this to show $\alpha = 0$ in $R_f$. Specifically, multiply by a high power to clear denominators.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Gluing
nodes.statement: \textbf{Surjectivity (Gluing):} Given compatible elements $(\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i}) \in \prod_i R_{f_i}$ (compatible means they agree on overlaps $D(f_i) \land D(f_j) = D(f_i f_j)$), we must construct a preimage in $R_f$. The compatibility says that on $D(f_i f_j)$, we have $\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i} = \alpha_j/f_j^{k_j}$, i.e., there exists $m_{ij}$ with $(f_i f_j)^{m_{ij}} (f_j^{k_j} \alpha_i - f_i^{k_i} \alpha_j) = 0$. Use a partition of unity in $R_f$ (obtained from $f^n = \sum_i r_i f_i$) to glue: $$\alpha/f^N := \sum_i (r_i/f^n) \cdot (\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i}) \quad \text{(in } R_f\text{)}$$ This element restricts to $(\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i})$ on each $D(f_i)$ by the partition of unity property.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Compatible family
nodes.statement: \textbf{Surjectivity (Gluing):} Given compatible elements $(\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i}) \in \prod_i R_{f_i}$ (compatible means they agree on overlaps $D(f_i) \land D(f_j) = D(f_i f_j)$), we must construct a preimage in $R_f$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Unfold compatibility
nodes.statement: The compatibility says that on $D(f_i f_j)$, we have $\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i} = \alpha_j/f_j^{k_j}$, i.e., there exists $m_{ij}$ with $(f_i f_j)^{m_{ij}} (f_j^{k_j} \alpha_i - f_i^{k_i} \alpha_j) = 0$.
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Glue via partition of unity
nodes.statement: Use a partition of unity in $R_f$ (obtained from $f^n = \sum_i r_i f_i$) to glue: $$\alpha/f^N := \sum_i (r_i/f^n) \cdot (\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i}) \quad \text{(in } R_f\text{)}$$
nodes.section: 4.2 The Structure Sheaf on Zariski Locales

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This element restricts to $(\alpha_i/f_i^{k_i})$ on each $D(f_i)$ by the partition of unity property.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We need to verify that for every $D(f) \in \mathrm{Spec} R$, the stalk $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R, \overline{D(f)}}$ is a local ring.

nodes.name: Compute stalk
nodes.statement: The stalk at $D(f)$ is: $$\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec} R, \overline{D(f)}} = \lim_{D(g) \leq D(f)} R_g$$ This is an inverse limit of localizations.

nodes.name: Standard algebra
nodes.statement: By standard commutative algebra, this is a local ring (the maximal ideal is generated by elements that become zero in localizations at $g$ with $g \notin \mathfrak{p}$ for any prime $\mathfrak{p}$ containing $f$).

nodes.name: Category structure
nodes.statement: Morphisms of schemes are defined as morphisms of locally ringed locales. Composition and identities are inherited from the category of locales and sheaves.

nodes.name: Affine pieces
nodes.statement: An affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec} R$ has the full ring $R$ as a single affine open (this corresponds to $D(1) = \top$).

nodes.name: Unfold order
nodes.statement: In the frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$, the order is inclusion. So $\mathfrak{p} \leq I \lor J$ means $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq I \lor J = \sqrt{I + J}$.

nodes.name: Restate
nodes.statement: This means $\mathfrak{p}^n \subseteq I + J$ for some $n$... actually, $\mathfrak{p}$ is radical, so $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq \sqrt{I + J}$.

nodes.name: Primeness
nodes.statement: If every element of $\mathfrak{p}$ is in $I + J$, and $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime, then $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq I$ or $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq J$.

nodes.name: Appeal to standard criterion
nodes.statement: This is the standard prime ideal criterion.

nodes.name: Witness and frame-primeness
nodes.statement: The counterexample is witnessed by $R = \mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ and $I = (0)$ (the nilradical). The nilradical is frame-prime because $\bot \leq J \vee K$ implies $\bot \leq J$ or $\bot \leq K$ trivially.

nodes.name: Not ring-prime
nodes.statement: However, the nilradical is not ring-prime because $2 \cdot 3 = 0 \in (0)$ but $2 \notin (0)$ and $3 \notin (0)$ (since neither $2$ nor $3$ is nilpotent in $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$).
